recipes.name: inbox-idle-reviewer
recipes.title: inbox-idle-reviewer
recipes.summary: When the Reviewer sits idle with unread mail, wakes its running session to claim the oldest ready PR and review it.
recipes.source:
# config/agents/reviewer/routines/inbox-idle-reviewer/routine.yml
id: inbox-idle-reviewer
name: Review the oldest ready PR
owner: codesense
mode: wake
task: |
  You have unread mail. Call read_messages with your session id, then
  claim_role_messages for the reviewer role. Review the oldest ready PR
  with bmad-code-review. If nothing is ready, say so in one line and wait.
where:
  kind: team_workspace
  machine: local
triggers:
  - event:
      kind: inbox_idle
policy:
  max_runtime: 30m
runs_on: each_mac
revision: 1

# A light check: no wake limits needed (a heavy one would set policy.min_gap,
# max_wakes_per_day or max_wakes). With machine: any, a Manager on a
# machine that is offline counts as running: the wake is undelivered
# (machine_offline) and no second Manager starts while that machine stays
# offline.
id: manager-ensure
name: Keep a manager on the queue
owner: codesense
mode: wake
task: |
  Check the manager queue. Call role_state with role "manager".
  If anything is pending, claim it with claim_role_messages and carry on
  with /manage-team. If nothing is pending, say "manager queue empty" in
  one line and wait.
where:
  kind: team_workspace
  machine: any
triggers:
  - schedule:
      cron: "0 * * * *"
      tz: UTC
policy:
  max_runtime: 5m
  overlap: skip
revision: 1

recipes.name: add-machine-user
recipes.title: add-machine-user
recipes.summary: Give a teammate SSH access to a remote machine for CodeSense — their own Unix account, or their key on a shared account.
recipes.source:
---
name: add-machine-user
description: Give a teammate SSH access to a remote machine for CodeSense — their own Unix account, or their key on a shared account. Use when the user says "add <name> to the build box", "/add-machine-user", "give my teammate access to <host>" or "authorize this key". Safe to rerun; it never adds a key twice.
---

# Add a teammate to a machine

You run on the user's Mac and change the remote machine over SSH, as plain shell. You need the
teammate's **public** key (a line starting `ssh-ed25519` or `ssh-rsa`, usually from their
`~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub`). A public key is safe to paste in chat.

Rules:

- Never ask for or accept a private key, a password or a token. If the user pastes something
  that isn't a single public key line, stop and say so.
- Ask before creating an account and before any `sudo` command. Show the exact command first.
- Check before you change. Running this twice must not add a second account or a duplicate
  key.
- Never remove an account or a key here unless the user asks, and confirm first.

## 1. Which machine, who, and how

Ask for:

- the SSH host (as in `~/.ssh/config`, or `user@host`);
- the teammate's name for the account (lowercase, such as `sam`);
- their public key;
- **own account** or **shared account**.

Recommend their **own account**. In CodeSense each person connects with a private account:
their own Unix login, their own files and their own agent logins. A **shared account** means
everyone works as the same Unix user and can see and change each other's files. Use it only
if the team already works that way: CodeSense itself needs each person's own account, and
opens no terminal tabs on a shared one.

Check the machine answers: `ssh -o BatchMode=yes <host> 'uname -s'`.

## 2a. Own account

Check whether it exists: `ssh <host> 'id -u <name>'`.

If it doesn't, ask, then create it (Linux; this needs `sudo`):

```sh
ssh -t <host> 'sudo useradd -m -s /bin/bash <name>'
```

On macOS use **System Settings → Users & Groups** on the machine, or `sudo sysadminctl -addUser
<name>`. Don't set a password: they sign in with their key.

Then add their key, without duplicating it:

```sh
ssh -t <host> 'k="<public key>"; f=~<name>/.ssh/authorized_keys
  sudo install -d -m 700 -o <name> ~<name>/.ssh
  sudo touch "$f" && sudo chown <name> "$f" && sudo chmod 600 "$f"
  sudo grep -qxF "$k" "$f" || echo "$k" | sudo tee -a "$f" >/dev/null'
```

## 2b. Shared account

The account is the one in `<host>`. Add their key, without duplicating it:

```sh
ssh <host> 'mkdir -p ~/.ssh && chmod 700 ~/.ssh && touch ~/.ssh/authorized_keys && chmod 600 ~/.ssh/authorized_keys && (grep -qxF "<public key>" ~/.ssh/authorized_keys || echo "<public key>" >> ~/.ssh/authorized_keys)'
```

No `sudo` is needed.

## 3. Check and hand over

Confirm the key is there once:
`ssh <host> 'sudo grep -cxF "<public key>" ~<name>/.ssh/authorized_keys'` (own account) or
the same `grep -c` without `sudo` on the shared account. It should print `1`.

You can't test their login from here: it uses their key. Tell the user to send the teammate:

- the host, port and their user name;
- to add it in CodeSense with **Machines → Add machine**, or to ask their agent to run
  `/setup-machine`, which ends with the `test_machine_connection` check.

If the team shares machines in CodeSense, the machine can also be saved for the team with
`save_machine` and a `team` share, so teammates see it in their list.

## 4. Summary

Say what you created or added, what was already there, and what the teammate does next.

Teams that already manage accounts with Ansible can keep doing that. This skill is just the
plain-shell version.

recipes.name: agent
recipes.title: agent
recipes.summary: Set up and manage the user's CodeSense agents — named, reusable workers (a runtime, its args, MCP servers, the content it starts with, and its permissions) the user and their team launch or run from routines.
recipes.source:
---
name: agent
description: Set up and manage the user's CodeSense agents — named, reusable workers (a runtime, its args, MCP servers, the content it starts with, and its permissions) the user and their team launch or run from routines. Use when the user says "make an agent that…", "set up a triage agent", "what agents do we have", "let it use Slack but not edit files", or asks to change, copy, archive or restore one. Advisory — the agent_* tools work without it.
---

# Agents

An agent is a named worker defined once and reused: which CLI runs it, the
extra args it gets, the MCP servers it can reach, the content paths it starts
with, its permissions, and an optional default prompt. It lives as
`config/agents/<id>/agent.yaml` in the context repo, revisioned on every save.
An Only me agent is private to the user; a team agent is one every teammate
can use and edit. The `agent_*` tools do all the work; this is how to use them
well.

One call makes a working agent:

```json
agent_create { "name": "Reviewer", "runtime": "claude" }
```

Everything else is optional and has a sensible default. `sessionId` is
optional on every tool: pass your `$CODESENSE_TAB_SESSION_ID` when CodeSense
launched you, so your revisions are credited to you (and `runtime` may then be
left out to mean your own CLI, when CodeSense recorded which); if you have
none, leave it out and always pass `runtime`.

```yaml
id: slack-triage
name: Slack triage
description: Sweeps #support and files actionable issues.
runtime: claude
launch: headless
mcp:
  servers: [slack]
startup:
  - CLAUDE.md
  - .claude/skills/triage/
permissions:
  claude:
    allow: ["Read", "Grep", "Glob", "mcp__slack__*"]
    deny: ["Edit", "Write", "Bash"]
default_prompt: /triage
```

## The starters: Claude, Codex and OpenCode

CodeSense ships three agents everyone has: `builtin/claude` ("Claude"),
`builtin/codex` ("Codex") and `builtin/opencode` ("OpenCode"). OpenCode runs
on this Mac only. Each runs its CLI with its defaults and the user's
own login: no extra args, no MCP server beyond the bridge, the CLI's own
permission config and no default prompt, so the user types the task. Each
starts with what CodeSense needs plus the team's root `CLAUDE.md` (Claude) or
`AGENTS.md` (Codex and OpenCode) when the team has one.

They are read-only: `agent_update`, `agent_delete`, `agent_restore` and
`agent_unarchive` reply `read_only`. To customize one, copy it (below) and
change the copy. A routine (Only me or team) may name either one.

## Compare existing agents first

Before creating one, call `agent_list` and read the names, descriptions and
`startup_count`s. If one already fits, use it. If one nearly fits, update it
with `agent_update` (a team agent is any teammate's to change). Don't make a
near-duplicate.

`scope: "mine"` on `agent_list` only narrows the view to your Only me agents
and the team agents you created. It is not a permission: every agent the
default `all` lists is yours to use and change.

### Copying an agent

There is no copy tool; get it, then create it. If the user wants their own
variant ("copy it to mine"), a starter included:

1. `agent_get {id}` and take its `definition`.
2. `agent_create` with that definition, minus `created_by`, `revision` and
   `archived_at` (CodeSense sets those), with `mcp: {servers: [..]}` passed as
   `mcpServers: [..]`, your change applied, and `scope: "personal"` with the
   `org` it goes in (the default scope is `team`). Keep or change `id`; it only
   has to be free where it goes.

A key the tool doesn't take is refused by name, with what to send instead,
so nothing you meant to copy is silently dropped.

## The fields

- `runtime`: `claude`, `codex` or `opencode`. These are the built-in CLIs. Pass it. It may
  be left out only when you pass `sessionId` and CodeSense knows which CLI
  launched you; otherwise leaving it out is an `invalid` reply naming
  `runtime`, never a guess.
- `args`: extra CLI argv words, one string each (`["--model", "opus"]`),
  never a command line.
- `launch`: `foreground` (a visible tab, the default) or `headless`.
- `mcpServers`: which servers from the team's MCP config (`.mcp.json`, or
  `.codex/config.toml`) the agent gets. The CodeSense bridge is always there,
  so never list it. Default: none beyond the bridge.
- `startup`: the content the agent starts with (below).
- `permissions`: the runtime's own permission config (below).
- `defaultPrompt`: what a launch starts with when the launcher gives nothing.

## Startup: plain content paths

`startup:` is an ordered list of content-relative paths. Each is a file, or a
directory that brings everything under it. There are no `skill:` or
`command:` keys: a skill is its directory, a command is its file.

```yaml
startup:
  [
    CLAUDE.md,
    .claude/skills/bmad-build/,
    .claude/commands/bmad-help.md,
    finish-codesense/02-routines/README.md,
  ]
```

The path rules (a save refuses anything else, naming the path):

- relative to the team's content root: no absolute paths;
- no `..`;
- no globs (`*`, `?`, `[`, `]`);
- not inside a reserved top-level dir (such as `.git`);
- no duplicates, and no entry inside another entry.

A file can name what it needs with optional `requires:` frontmatter. Its
values are content paths too, and they come along whenever the file does:

```yaml
---
name: triage
requires: [.claude/commands/bmad-help.md]
---
```

Default `startup` is empty: the agent gets only what CodeSense itself needs.

A path no content layer has is a manifest error, with one exception: the
runtime's root instructions file (`CLAUDE.md` for claude, `AGENTS.md` for
codex and opencode). Where the team has none, the agent simply starts without it, as the
starters do.

### Slash commands must be in startup

A prompt or a routine task is passed verbatim. If it starts with `/name`, the
agent needs `.claude/commands/name.md` or `.claude/skills/name/` among its
startup paths (codex: `.agents/skills/name/`). Otherwise the run won't find
the command. `agent_get` and `agent_preview` list what the agent `provides`,
and warn when the default prompt names something it doesn't start with.

### When startup takes effect

Named local product launches apply the resolved startup manifest before spawning.
Story, remote, and other launch paths retain their existing context behavior.
`manifest_applies_at_launch` remains false because this capability is not universal.
Existing files remain available; startup selections do not prune old context.
Permissions apply per launch on all these paths.

## MCP servers and permissions

`mcpServers` picks which servers exist for the agent. **Permissions** say what
it may do with them and with its built-in tools. They are the runtime's own
native config, enforced by the CLI and never by CodeSense, and passed through
verbatim. They apply per launch: Claude gets them through its own `--settings`
file, Codex through its own scoped home, so they never leak to another agent
launched in the same folder. CodeSense only adds the allows its own tools
need (`signal_done` and friends); a rule that blocks those is kept as written
and only warned about.

Claude takes `{claude: {allow, ask, deny, additionalDirectories, defaultMode,
disableBypassPermissionsMode}}` with Claude's own rule strings. Codex takes
`{codex: {approvalPolicy, sandboxMode}}`. OpenCode takes `{opencode:
{permission}}`, OpenCode's own permission map. A key the agent's runtime doesn't
have is refused, naming `permissions.<runtime>.<key>`.

A triage agent that is read-only plus Slack:

```json
{
  "name": "Slack triage",
  "runtime": "claude",
  "mcpServers": ["slack"],
  "permissions": {
    "claude": {
      "allow": ["Read", "Grep", "Glob", "mcp__slack__*"],
      "deny": ["Edit", "Write", "Bash"]
    }
  }
}
```

A dev agent that may build and test but not force-push:

```json
{
  "name": "Dev",
  "runtime": "claude",
  "permissions": {
    "claude": {
      "allow": ["Bash(npm run build:*)", "Bash(npm test:*)", "Edit"],
      "deny": ["Bash(git push --force:*)", "Bash(git push -f:*)"]
    }
  }
}
```

The codex equivalent of the dev agent:

```json
{
  "name": "Dev (codex)",
  "runtime": "codex",
  "permissions": { "codex": { "approvalPolicy": "on-request", "sandboxMode": "workspace-write" } }
}
```

With no permissions the CLI's own defaults apply. A headless Codex agent with
no policy gets `approval_policy = "never"` and `sandbox_mode =
"workspace-write"` when unset, so it can't hang on an approval nobody sees.
The bypass flag is never added for you: it applies only if the agent's own
`args` carry it.

Routines can **wake** an agent: type their task into its running session
instead of starting a new one. That needs `launch: foreground` (a headless run
is never woken), and an agent that auto-approves every tool (a bypass flag in
`args`, or `bypassPermissions` mode) is woken only if it also sets
`allowWake: true`. Without it, its
routines start a new session each time.

An agent can **resume after a terminal server update**: with
`resumeAfterRestart: true`, a session the update ended is relaunched as the
same agent, in its workspace and tab, with a resume brief CodeSense builds
from its own records (its last `signal_progress` and `signal_done`, its inbox,
its routine run, the git state and the terminal's last lines; secrets
redacted, at most 8 KB). It never relies on a CLI session id, so it works the
same for Claude, Codex and any other runtime. Off by default. Without it, the
tab reopens as a shell — as it does when the relaunch is refused (its
workspace or launch folder is gone, or a This Mac launch ran outside a
CodeSense-managed folder). A relaunch runs the agent as saved: a launch's own
mode, account or extra arguments are not carried over.

## No limits, only warnings

CodeSense never caps an agent. A long startup list, a huge directory, many
MCP servers or broad permissions are all saved as given. What looks off comes
back in `warnings` (and in `manifest.totals` / `manifest.errors`): an unusually
large entry or manifest, build output or binaries in a startup directory, a
`/name` the agent doesn't start with, or permissions that block CodeSense's
own tools. Pass them on to the user; they decide.

## The account is per user

Which Claude or Codex login runs the agent is not part of the definition.
Each user runs it with their own CLI login (the account they bound it to on
their own Mac, else their active account for the runtime). There is no
account field and no tool input for one: never put an account in
`agent.yaml`. `resolved.account` shows which login the current user would
launch it with; binding a different one is each user's own choice on their
Mac.

## "Make an agent that…"

1. `agent_list`: does one already fit? (See "Compare existing agents first".)
2. `agent_preview` with the fields you will create it with (it takes exactly
   `agent_create`'s fields). Check `manifest.errors`, `warnings`, and that
   `provides` has every `/name` its prompts use. Fix and preview again.
3. `agent_create` with the same fields. It goes to the team by default; pass
   `scope: "personal"` and `org` only when the user wants it for themselves
   (Only me). `dryRun: true` returns the
   same reply and writes nothing.
4. Tell the user its `id`, what it starts with, and any warning.

A validation error is `{ok: false, error: {code: "invalid", message, field}}`
and writes nothing; fix the named `field` and call again.

## Changing, archiving and restoring

- `agent_update` takes the `revision` you last read as `baseRevision`, plus
  only the fields that change. An explicit `[]` clears a list. A
  `permissions` runtime block you send replaces that block whole; `null`
  removes them all.
- A `conflict` reply (`current_revision`) means it changed since you read it.
  Nothing was written: `agent_get` it again and reapply the change.
- `agent_delete` archives it: it drops out of lists and pickers, and its own
  routines (the ones under `config/agents/<id>/routines/`) are archived with it.
  With active routines it is refused `needs_confirm`, listing them: confirm
  with the user, then pass `archiveRoutines: true`. Routines that only wait on
  it (`agent_done from_agent`) keep resolving. `agent_unarchive` brings it
  back and offers its routines. `hard: true` removes it for good, refused
  (`in_use`) while it has active routines or routines wait on it.
- `used_by` and `in_use` list only the routines you can see. A teammate's
  Only me routine can run a team agent and is invisible to you, so a hard
  delete of a team agent may still strand hidden routines: their runs then
  fail `agent_unavailable` until their owner names another agent. Archive a
  team agent instead of hard-deleting it unless the user is sure.
- `agent_restore` makes an old revision current again; `agent_unarchive`
  brings an archived agent back.

Any agent you can see is yours to change, a teammate's team agent included.
Each revision is credited to whoever made it.

## Edits are local until pushed

Every create, update, archive or restore is a local edit to the context repo
on this Mac. Teammates get it when the user's agent pushes it with git, which
is yours to do when the user wants it. CodeSense never commits or pushes it
for you, and creating or changing an agent tells no one.

recipes.summary: Design a small CodeSense agent team with the user.
recipes.source:
---
name: agent-design
description: Design a small CodeSense agent team with the user. Use when asked to "set up my agents", "design a team", "what agents should I have", or improve an existing team. Discover, propose, preview, ask before saving, prove and hand over.
---

# Agent design

Use CodeSense MCP tools. You do not need CodeSense source. The playbook is
[Agent design](../../../arc-e-agents/agent-design.html). Cite the page and section
used at each step. Read the running tool's input schema before calling it. If docs
and the running app differ, report the mismatch and follow the tool contract.

## 1. Orient

Call `codesense_overview`. Read its docs location and version information when
present; do not invent a version if absent. Read the guide above. To find the
installed guide, use `query_context` with
`where: {orgs: ["codesense/docs"]}` and `text: "agent design"`. Read the matching
page using its returned path, with `read_rendered_document` or an available file
reader. Resolve a mismatch between docs and the app before changing the setup.

Call `describe_setup`, `agent_list` and `routine_list`. Read reusable definitions
with `agent_get`. Find CodeSense tools with `codesense_search_tools`. Report errors
in the current setup before editing that part of it.

## 2. Interview

Follow the guide's **Discover the work and data** section. Ask at most three
questions at once. Stop when you can write a useful design:

- What repeats, how often, and what result counts as good?
- What needs a human? What may happen unattended? What are the hard limits?
- Which tools, repos and machines are involved?
- Where does data live, who owns it, and how sensitive is it? Does this task need
  read or write access? Which MCP servers and tools are actually connected?
- What is the time and money budget? What should the user see and how do they pause it?

Minimize data and access per seat. Prefer selected fields, counts and ids over raw
personal records. Never request secrets in chat or copy them into design files.

## 3. Propose

Follow **Shape the smallest team** and **Choose models and budgets**. Prefer fixed
scripts, checks and command routines before model calls. Offer one or two patterns
with trade-offs. Start with one seat when it can do the job.

Show a table: seat, agent, model choice, role, routine, pane, tool access or grants,
risk tier and why. Add cost assumptions, autonomy limits, stop conditions and proof
cases. Compare model quality, speed and cost on the task; use `model_rates` and
`session_usage` when available. Missing prices are unknown, not zero. Choose by
task type, not by a blanket Claude or Codex ranking.

Show a **dry-run plan**: exact previews, proposed saved resources, expected outputs,
what would launch or cost money, and what will stay disabled. Read-only previews
may run now. Get the user's explicit approval of the design and plan before saving
anything or launching a proof. Existing approval applies only to its stated scope.

## 4. Record

Follow **Write the design down**. After approval, write a short design note in
content the user owns. Record goals, data sensitivity, decisions and their reasons,
seats, tool boundaries, budget, risk tiers, handoffs, proof cases and who approved.
Keep a list of created ids so the user can change or remove the setup.

The optional `team-design.yaml` and human-readable `DESIGN.md` are a structured
record of intent. Use the plain note unless the user already has that format. Refer to agents and routines by id. Do not duplicate
fields from their real `agent.yaml` and `routine.yml`. Never save data or secrets
in a design. Keep personal and finance notes in the private layer.

## 5. Apply

Follow **Build in small steps**, in this order:

1. Agents: prefer reuse or a copy. Call `agent_preview`, check manifest errors,
   warnings, context and provided skills. Use `agent_create` with `dryRun: true`
   before saving. Do not proceed with unresolved errors. Keep returned ids.
2. Roles: newer apps offer `role_save`; check the running tool list. If absent,
   copy the starter's matching role YAML. Use the selected team key and role
   config. A default handler does not launch itself. A worker still registers with `register_role`.
3. Routines: use `routine_create` with `dryRun: true`, then save with
   `enabled: false`. Bind the actual saved agent. Newer apps support command
   actions, argv commands, metadata triggers and `after` through MCP. Check the
   running schema; if advanced fields are absent, use an approved schedule-only
   agent routine that checks state. Event
   triggers such as role-pending currently need YAML. Read the
   [solo-founder walkthrough](../../agents/solo-founder/README.md) before copying
   its wake routine. Never invent an unsupported event parameter. If
   `open_workspace` lacks its queue-selection field, omit that field and keep
   explicit `register_role` in the saved prompt.
4. Panes: only if needed, use `pane_write` with the agreed capabilities and grants.
5. Inheritance: only if needed and approved, use `set_team_parent`. Only content
   follows the parent chain. Parent config does not become child config.
   A child receives only the content paths its ancestors declare in `config/sharing.yml`;
   each team in between must share them onward.
   Preview from the child team.

Name every resource clearly. Add only startup/context paths that exist for this
user. Never assume a workflow skill or external MCP server is installed. Use the
starter's self-contained prompts when they fit. Saving is a local context-repo
edit; sharing through git is a separate action. Ask before enabling each routine.

## 6. Prove

Follow **Prove it works**. A creation dry run validates setup and writes nothing.
`routine_run_now` performs real work; it has no dry-run flag.

After approval, run one bounded end-to-end normal case and one stop case per seat.
Send labelled test work with `send_role_message`. Verify registration, claim,
acceptance, acknowledgement and the final result. Check the handoff in a fresh
session, with the selected context. Confirm that missing approval stops action.

Inspect `routine_runs` and `routine_run`. For story runs, use `list_runs` and
`read_run_evidence` when evidence exists. Open an optional pane with `pane_open` and
check the visible result. Show the user the evidence and any unverified behavior.
A preview is not proof of a live handoff. On failure, pause, simplify and retry the
bounded case; ask the user when the agreed retry budget is exhausted.

## 7. Hand over

Give the user the design location, saved ids, what runs when, expected spend and
what needs approval. Show how to pause with `routine_set_enabled`, and how to read
or change definitions with `agent_get` and `agent_update` using the current revision.
Explain how to remove this setup without touching other work. Report what was
proved, what remains disabled and what still needs a real run.

## 8. Revisit

Follow **Iterate from evidence** and **Learning and context**. Offer a manual weekly
or monthly review, or an optional review routine within the user's budget. Ask
before scheduling it. Read structured usage and outcome signals, compare with the
goals, and propose one change at a time. Replay the agreed cases before applying.

A fuller loop adds a fresh-context evaluator and a steward that proposes changes
for approval. Its monthly memory prune keeps, merges, summarizes or archives notes
within a per-agent context budget. It does not auto-apply policy. Use small notes
with provenance. Quarantine untrusted-source facts until a human promotes them.
Keep personal and finance memory private. This skill does not install evaluator or
steward skills.

## Guardrails

- CodeSense provides mechanisms. The user and agents choose policy. Do not present
  a pattern, model choice or workflow as an engine requirement.
- Save and launch only within the approved design. Confirm new schedules, paid
  work and any wider access. A preview does not authorize creation.
- Safety tiers: R0 reads and analyses. R1 makes bounded, reversible private drafts.
  R2 outward actions need explicit human approval of content, recipients and
  limits. R3 money movement, trading and deletion need explicit approval of the
  exact action and hard limits. Keep R2/R3 actions out of unattended seats.
- Tiers and prompts are not runtime enforcement. Restrict tools and native CLI
  permissions. Do not give one agent or an unbounded message chain both untrusted
  input, sensitive data and outward tools. Use validated ids and bounded fields.
- Keep the design in content the user owns. Only content inherits today; do not
  promise config inheritance or treat a parent relationship as a privacy boundary.
- Claude agents call `who_am_i` with no arguments. Their MCP connection supplies
  `sessionId` for `who_am_i`, `signal_done` and `routine_publish_result` when
  omitted. Headless permissions can deny shell variable expansion, so a Claude
  seat's bootstrap must not depend on `echo`.
- Codex agents pass your own sessionId to `send_message`/`signal_done`.
  The wire key is `session_id` for `send_message` and `reply`, and `sessionId` for
  `signal_done`. For every `send_role_message`, set `sender` to your own handle
  from `who_am_i.handle`. First run
  `echo $CODESENSE_TAB_SESSION_ID` in your shell. If empty, match your own tab name
  and workspace in `list_sessions` and take `launchTelemetry.sessionId`. If there
  is no unique match, ask instead of guessing. Pass that id to `who_am_i` and
  keep its returned handle for role-message attribution and replies. Inspect the
  running schema. Never send as an implied human or another
  session.
- To stop future starts, call `routine_set_enabled` with `enabled: false` for each
  routine. To stop running sessions, take each intended `handle` from
  `list_sessions`, then call `close_terminal_tab` with that handle. It ends the
  CLI and keeps the worktree files. These are separate actions; do not promise
  a single kill switch. Close only sessions the user intended to stop.
- Keep scope and release decisions with the user. Pause on unclear approval.
  Never claim proof from configuration, a dry run or missing evidence.

recipes.summary: Walk the user through setting up CodeSense — workspace, teams, source repos, agents and routines — using the CodeSense MCP tools.
recipes.source:
---
name: codesense-setup
description: Walk the user through setting up CodeSense — workspace, teams, source repos, agents and routines — using the CodeSense MCP tools. Use when the user says "set up CodeSense", "/codesense-setup", "what's left to set up", or "add my repos". Safe to rerun; it reports what is done and what is left.
---

# CodeSense setup

You set CodeSense up with the user by calling the `codesense` MCP tools. CodeSense
only records and shows the setup. You do the work and you check with the user first.

Rules:

- Start by calling `describe_setup`, and call it again after each section. Its result is
  the source of truth. Don't rely on what you remember. If something is already done, say
  so and move on. A rerun only does what is still left.
- Ask before you change anything. Ask before you clone, create, rename or add something,
  and confirm the exact names with the user.
- Get an explicit "yes" before any destructive step. These are `delete_team`,
  `archive_team`, `remove_source_repo` and a hard `agent_delete`. Say exactly what will
  happen first.
- Never ask for a token, password or API key in chat, and never accept one. CodeSense
  stores no service credentials; external services are reached through the user's own
  tools and logins.
- Every tool returns `{status, ...}`. A `validation` or `unauthorizedTeam` status carries
  the reason in plain language. Show it to the user, fix the input, and don't retry
  blindly.
- Keep it short. One section at a time, a line or two per step.

## 1. Discover

Call `describe_setup`. It returns:

- `activeOrg` and `activeTeam`.
- `orgs[]`. Each org has its teams. Each team has its `sourceRepos` (with their
  `attachment` and `localPath`).
- `scratch`. The user's private space (**Private** in the app): things only they use. `scratch.orgs[]` has one
  entry per org with what is filed for that org (notes, files, dashboards, routines,
  agents), and `scratch.allOrgs` counts the skills, prompts,
  snippets and templates that apply in every org. Nothing here needs setting up.

Give the user a short checklist of what's done and what's left, then ask where to start.
Default to the order below.

## 2. Workspace

- **No org in `orgs`.** Nothing else can be set up yet. If your tool list includes
  `create_local_organization`, offer to create a local organization with it; if it
  includes `attach_context_repository`, offer to attach an existing context repo instead.
  Otherwise ask the user to create or attach one in the CodeSense app, then rerun this
  skill.
- **An org lists `loadErrors`.** Report them. Don't edit that org.
- To rename a workspace, call `rename_workspace {org, name}`. The slug stays the same.
- If the user has more than one org, ask which one to work in. Pass that org's `slug` as
  `org` everywhere below.

## 3. Teams

- To create a team, call `create_team {org, name, parent?, activate?}`. The name is a
  lowercase slug. Set `activate: true` when the user wants to work in the new team now.
- To switch teams, call `set_active_team {org, team}`.
- To rename, call `rename_team {org, team, newName}`. To nest or un-nest, call
  `set_team_parent {org, team, parent?}`.
- Archiving with `archive_team {org, team, archived}` can be undone.
  `delete_team {org, team}` removes the team from the registry. Its content stays on disk.
  Confirm both with the user first.

## 4. Source repos

Each team tracks the code repos it works on. For each repo the user names, check the
team's `sourceRepos`:

- **Attached** (`attachment: attached`). Done.
- **Already cloned on this machine.** Call `add_source_repo {org, team, path}` with the
  absolute path of the clone's root. That adds the repo and binds the clone. If the team
  already tracks the repo, use `attach_source_repo_path {org, team, repo, path}` instead.
  `missing` and `unattached` repos are fixed the same way.
- **Not cloned yet.** CodeSense never clones. Ask the user where to put it, run
  `git clone <url> <dir>` yourself, then add it by `path` as above.
- **Track it now, clone later.** Call `add_source_repo {org, team, url}`.
- If the result asks for an `account` (several code-host accounts fit), ask the user which
  account to use and pass its id.
- To check the result, call `list_source_repos`. `remove_source_repo {org, team, repo}`
  stops tracking a repo and leaves the clone on disk. Confirm it first.

## 5. Agents and routines

- Call `agent_list`. Everyone has the two starters, `builtin/claude` and `builtin/codex`,
  so a team needs no agent of its own to start. If the user wants a named worker (a
  reviewer, a triage agent), make it with `agent_create`; its description lists every
  field. Prefer updating or copying an agent that already fits.
- For anything that should run on a schedule ("every weekday at 9…"), call
  `routine_create` with the agent it belongs to and a `mode`: `wake` delivers the task into
  that agent's running session (starting one only if none runs), `fresh` starts a new one
  each time. Its description covers the schedule forms and what the task must say. For a
  one-off reminder in the current session ("check back in 20 minutes"), use
  `schedule_wakeup` instead: a timer that ends with the session.
- Agents and routines go to the team by default, where every teammate can see and change
  them. When the user wants one for themselves, pass `scope: "personal"` and the `org`: it
  lands in their private space for that org (Only me) and never applies in another org.
- Creating either is a local edit to the context repo. The team gets it when the user's
  agent pushes it with git.

For a team with several seats or unclear handoffs, follow the
[agent-design guide](../../../arc-e-agents/agent-design.html) and
[agent-design skill](../agent-design/SKILL.md). Start with discovery and a written
proposal. Preview before saving, and ask before creating or enabling anything.

## 6. Summary

Call `describe_setup` one last time. Report what this run changed, what is still left,
and anything that is waiting on the user in the app, such as a workspace to attach.

recipes.summary: Move context between this workspace and team content on request. Pull team files into the workspace, or publish the workspace's edits back after a preview.
recipes.source:
---
name: context-sync
description: Move context between this workspace and team content on request. Pull team files into the workspace, or publish the workspace's edits back after a preview. Use when the user says "pull the latest skills", "bring in this story's epic", "publish my edits to the team", "what would publishing change", or "add this file to team context". Example from the CodeSense docs — when you copy it into your context repo's `.claude/skills/`, delete this sentence and adapt the rest. The CodeSense MCP tools work without it.
---

# Context sync

CodeSense never syncs on its own. A workspace gets context when it is created and when an
agent starts in it; anything more happens only when you call one of these tools. This skill
just picks the right one and always previews before it writes team content.

`hydrate_worktree`, `hydrate_story`, `preview_reverse_sync_worktree`,
`reverse_sync_worktree` and `list_hydrated` take a `target`. On This Mac:
`target: {"kind": "local", "codeRepoPath": "$PWD", "sessionId": "$CODESENSE_TAB_SESSION_ID"}`.
On a machine: `{"kind": "remote", "machineId": "…", "workspaceHandle": "…"}`.
Routing takes paths instead (This Mac only), and `context_operation_status` and
`cancel_context_operation` take an `operationId`; both are below.

## Pull team context in

- Named files or folders: `hydrate_worktree` with `paths` (exact files) or `sets` (folders
  such as `".claude/skills"`). It adds what is missing and refreshes what nobody edited.
  A file you edited is kept and reported, never overwritten.
- A story's epic: `hydrate_story` with `storyId`.
- Only pass `prune: true` when the user asks to remove copies the workspace no longer
  wants. It acts only under the `paths`/`sets` of that call (with neither, the runtime
  defaults: `CLAUDE.md`, `.claude/{commands,hooks,agents,skills}`, `AGENTS.md`,
  `.agents/skills`) and never removes an edited file.
- Only pass `overwriteModified: true` when the user asks to discard their edits to those
  files, and always with `paths` naming exactly those files.

## Publish edits back

1. Call `preview_reverse_sync_worktree` with the same `target`, `paths` and `sets` you
   will publish. Show the user the entries, conflicts and `withheldRemovals`.
2. Ask before publishing. On a yes, call `reverse_sync_worktree` with the same inputs.
3. A conflict is never written: the team file changed since it was copied. To resolve one:
   1. Save the workspace's version of the file somewhere outside the workspace.
   2. Call `hydrate_worktree` with `paths: [that file]` and `overwriteModified: true`. This
      takes the team's version and makes it the new base.
   3. Re-apply the saved edit on top of it.
   4. Preview again, then publish.

Team content is never deleted unless you pass `includeDeletes: true`. Pass it only when the
user asked to remove those team files and the preview showed them.

## Add one new file to team context

This Mac only. `route_file_to_context` with `codeRepoPath` (`$PWD`), `codeRepoSlug`
(`owner/repo`) and `logicalName` (the repo-relative path). It copies the file into team
content and hides it from git. `unroute_file_from_context`, with the same three, undoes it.

## Long operations

`hydrate_worktree`, `hydrate_story` and `reverse_sync_worktree` accept an `operationId` (a
UUID): calling again with the same one returns the kept result, so a retry is safe.
`context_operation_status` and `cancel_context_operation` take that `operationId`; a
cancel stops the operation without leaving a partial file. `list_hydrated` shows what
CodeSense copied into this workspace.

recipes.name: manage-team
recipes.title: manage-team
recipes.summary: Run as the team's manager. Hold the `manager` role queue, triage what arrives, launch workers and track them, and report to the human.
recipes.source:
---
name: manage-team
description: Run as the team's manager. Hold the `manager` role queue, triage what arrives, launch workers and track them, and report to the human. Use when launched as the Manager agent, or when the user says "/manage-team", "be the manager" or "take over the manager queue".
---

# Manage the team

You are the team's manager. CodeSense does not know that: to it you are an ordinary agent
holding a role it calls `manager`. Everything a manager does here is built from tools any agent
has. Work goes into the queue, you take it out, decide, act or delegate, and keep the human
informed. The queue is your memory, so a fresh session of you can always pick up where the
last one stopped.

## 1. Find out who you are and join the queue

1. Your session id is `$CODESENSE_TAB_SESSION_ID`. Call `who_am_i {session_id}` for your
   `handle` (how others address you) and `displayName`.
2. Call `codesense_overview` and take `context.org` and `context.team`. Every role tool takes
   them as `team: {org, team}`.
3. Call `register_role {team, role: "manager", sessionId, exclusive: true}`.
   - `exclusive: true` makes the role one-holder-only: a second manager is refused.
   - On `{status: "alreadyHeld", instance}` (instance = the holding session), another session is already the manager. Tell the
     human who holds it (`send_message {to: "human", kind: "update"}`) and stop. Do not fight for it.
   - Otherwise keep `generation` from the reply. Your instance id is your session id: pass it
     as `instanceId` to every claim, accept, ack and release.
   - CodeSense keeps your registration alive for as long as this session runs, and releases
     it when the session ends. Do not heartbeat or re-register on a timer.

## 2. Finish what a previous manager left

`register_role` returns `acceptedUnacked`: work an earlier manager accepted but never
finished. Your first `claim_role_messages` hands those back with `existingReceipt`. Finish each
one (check its state with `list_sessions` and `inbox_list`, it may already be done), then
`ack_role_message` with that `receiptId`. Read your open-items note (step 6) before deciding.

## 3. The loop

Repeat while there is work:

1. `claim_role_messages {team, role: "manager", instanceId, generation, limit: 10}`. Each
   delivery has `deliveryId`, `messageId` and `claimToken`. Read the full text with
   `inbox_list {role: "manager", include: ["text"]}` (without `include`, a body over 2 KB
   comes as a `textPreview`).
2. Decide what each one is, then `accept_role_message {team, deliveryId, claimToken,
   instanceId, generation, disposition}`:
   - `disposition: {kind: "work"}` when you or a worker will act on it.
   - `disposition: {kind: "no_work", noteOrReason: "..."}` for a duplicate, an FYI, or
     something that needs nothing. Say why.
3. Act:
   - **Small or clear.** Do it yourself, then answer the sender with `reply {message_id, text,
     session_id}`.
   - **Real work.** Launch a worker (section 4).
   - **Needs a human decision.** `send_message {to: "human", text, session_id, kind:
     "needs-you", replyTo: "role:manager"}` (`kind: "needs-you"` marks it as waiting on the human for agent views
     and dashboards; a Reply-To naming your own role alone reads as an update): a short markdown question with the options and your recommendation.
     When there is state to show, send `contentType: "html"`, a live dashboard, with a
     one-line plain-text `summary` for the Inbox preview. The answer
     comes back to your queue. Never decide a merge, an approval or anything irreversible
     unless the team's `CLAUDE.md` says you may.
4. `ack_role_message {team, deliveryId, claimToken, instanceId, generation, receiptId}` with
   the `receiptId` from the accept. Ack when you have handled the delivery (answered it,
   handed it to a worker, asked the human), not when the underlying work is finished.

When a claim returns nothing, go to section 5, then wait. You do not need to poll: a wake
routine types into your session when mail arrives (see the recipe this skill came with). A
message that starts with `[routine: <name> | run <id>]` is such a wake: do what it says, then
`routine_done {sessionId, runId, outcome: "success"}`. To check something yourself later,
set a timer on your own session with `schedule_wakeup`.

## 4. Launch and brief workers

- **On this Mac:** `open_workspace {target: "story", story_id, name, agent, initial_prompt,
  launched_by: <your session id>}`, or `target: "team-workspace"` with a `name` for work that
  has no story. `agent` is a saved Agent from `agent_list`.
- **On a machine:** the same call with `machine_id` from `list_machines`. A remote worker has
  the same tools you do.
- `launched_by` makes the worker yours: it nests under you in the agents list, and
  `list_sessions {launched_by: <your handle>}` lists it.
- Brief it with `send_message {to: <its handle>, text, session_id, replyTo: "role:manager"}`.
  A brief says: the task, where the context is, the constraints, and what "done" looks like.
  End every brief with this line:

  > When you need the human, `send_message {to: "human", kind: "needs-you", replyTo:
  > "role:manager"}`. When you
  > finish or get stuck, `send_message` me. Then call `signal_done`.

`replyTo: "role:manager"` sends every answer to the manager queue instead of to the session
that asked. It still arrives if the worker, or you, have since exited. The human sees "Replies
go to: manager" under the message, so nothing is hidden.

## 5. Track workers and report

Between batches:

- `list_sessions {launched_by: <your handle>}` shows your workers with `state` (`running`,
  `idle`, `needs-you`, `exited`, `offline`), `progress` and `unread`.
- A worker in `needs-you` waits for a permission: tell the human which one.
- A worker `idle` with work left: `send_to_session {handle, text}` to nudge it.
- `read_messages {session_id}` drains mail sent to you directly.

Report to the human only when something changed that is worth a person's time: done, blocked,
needs you. Send one digest with `send_message {to: "human", kind: "update", replyTo:
"role:manager"}`, not one message per worker: it appears as a conversation in the human Inbox and counts in its badge until read. Send
what needs a decision separately, with `kind: "needs-you"`. Check `get_human_status` first: when the human is `busy` or
`offline`, save non-urgent news for later.

## 6. Keep a short open-items note

Write what is in flight to `manager/open-items.md` in team content: each worker's handle,
its task, and what you are waiting for. Read it at start and update it when it changes. Query
the state again with the tools rather than trusting the note: the note says where to look,
the tools say what is true.

## 7. When something is stale

- `StaleRegistration`: your registration lapsed (for example, the app was closed or your
  machine was offline). Call `register_role` again with the same arguments, then claim again.
- `StaleClaim` or `StaleAck`: that claim expired and another claim can take it. Claim again.

Nothing is lost: the deliveries live in the queue, not in your session.

## 8. Stopping

When the human asks you to stop, finish the current delivery, then call `release_role {team,
role: "manager", instanceId, generation}`. Claimed work you had not accepted goes back to
pending for the next manager.

recipes.name: routine
recipes.title: routine
recipes.summary: Set up and manage the user's CodeSense routines and session timers. A routine is a saved, standing instruction an Agent runs on a schedule or an event ("make a routine for Barb to triage issues every weekday"); a timer is a temporary routine for the session you are in ("add a routine for your session to check the build in 20 minutes", "remind yourself").
recipes.source:
---
name: routine
description: Set up and manage the user's CodeSense routines and session timers. A routine is a saved, standing instruction an Agent runs on a schedule or an event ("make a routine for Barb to triage issues every weekday"); a timer is a temporary routine for the session you are in ("add a routine for your session to check the build in 20 minutes", "remind yourself"). Use when the user says "set this up as a routine", "do this every morning", "remind yourself", "check back on X", "what routines do I have", "pause X", "make it a draft", or asks to change, run or delete one. Advisory — the routine_* and *_wakeup tools work without it.
---

# Routines and timers

CodeSense has two ways to make an agent do something later. Pick by **who it is for**
and **how long it should last**:

| The user says                                                      | Make a…                    | Tool                                    |
| ------------------------------------------------------------------ | -------------------------- | --------------------------------------- |
| "add a routine for your session to check the build in 20 minutes"  | **timer** on your session  | `schedule_wakeup`                       |
| "remind yourself at 3pm to post the summary"                       | **timer**                  | `schedule_wakeup`                       |
| "check the deploy every 10 minutes until it's green"               | **timer** (repeating)      | `schedule_wakeup` with `every`          |
| "make a routine for Barb to triage new issues every weekday at 9"  | **routine** on Barb        | `routine_create` with `agent: "barb"`   |
| "every morning, start a fresh agent that writes the standup"       | **routine**, start a new   | `routine_create` with `mode: "fresh"`   |
| "whenever Barb has unread mail and is idle, wake her up"           | **routine**, `inbox_idle`  | a `routine.yml` with an event trigger   |

- A **timer** belongs to one running session: yours. It types its prompt into *this*
  conversation, so you keep your context. It never starts anything, never reaches another
  session, is never written to git, and **ends when the session ends** (exit, close, crash).
- A **routine** belongs to a saved **Agent**. It is a file in the team's context repo,
  `config/agents/<agent>/routines/<id>/routine.yml`, that outlives every session, shows
  under that agent in the **Agents** tab, and is shared with the team by a git push.

When in doubt about "your session" vs "Barb": if the user names an agent, or says
"every weekday" with no end, it is a routine. If they mean "you, right now, later", it is
a timer.

## Timers: "add a routine for your session"

One call to `schedule_wakeup`:

```json
{
  "sessionId": "$CODESENSE_TAB_SESSION_ID",
  "in": "20m",
  "name": "Check the build",
  "prompt": "Check the CI run for PR #212. If it is green, merge it; if red, read the failing job and fix it."
}
```

- `sessionId` is your own `$CODESENSE_TAB_SESSION_ID`. Another session's id is refused:
  a timer can only wake the session that set it.
- When: exactly one of `in` (`90s`, `20m`, `2h`, `1h30m`, `1d`) or `at` (RFC 3339 **with
  its offset**, in the future; `date +%z` prints yours). Add `every` (at least `1m`) to
  repeat, then at most one of `until` (RFC 3339) or `count` (at least 1). Add `minGap`
  (`30m`, `2h`; 1m to `7d`) when each fire starts heavy work: a fire inside the gap
  folds into the last one instead of waking you again.
- Write `prompt` for yourself later: it arrives as a new message, starting with
  `[timer: <name> | fire <n>]`, once you are idle. It is never typed while you are working
  or waiting on a permission prompt; fires due while one still waits collapse into it.
- `list_wakeups {sessionId}` shows your timers; `cancel_wakeup {sessionId, timerId}`
  stops one. Tell the user the `nextAt` you got back.
- Works in any interactive CodeSense session, saved agent or not, on this Mac or on a
  connected machine. Not for headless runs (`claude -p`) or Codex sessions. Setting, listing and cancelling need the CodeSense desktop connected; timers already
  set on a remote machine keep firing while the desktop is away. On a remote machine, if the
  desktop disconnects your CodeSense tools stop working for the rest of the session; your timers keep firing, but you can't list or cancel them until a restart.
- Limits: 10 active timers per session, 200 per machine. There is no lifetime cap: a
  session that runs for a week can take hundreds of small wakes. A fixed safety backstop
  (120 wakes an hour per session, every source together) refuses the rest as
  `rate_limited`, posts one inbox note naming the top source, and resumes on its own.

People set timers too: **Remind this agent…** in a terminal tab's menu. A tab with timers
shows a clock chip in its caption; its popover lists them with Cancel and **Keep this…**,
which turns a timer into a routine on the tab's agent (saving the session as an agent
first if it has none).

## Routines: "make a routine for Barb"

Every routine runs a saved **Agent** from `agent_list` (its runtime, MCP servers, startup
paths and permissions), and lives under it. Pick one, or make one first with
`agent_create`. One call to `routine_create`:

```json
{
  "name": "Morning triage",
  "agent": "barb",
  "mode": "wake",
  "when": "weekdays 09:00",
  "task": "Triage issues opened in acme/web since yesterday. Label each by area, post a 3-line summary to #web-triage with the Slack MCP tools, then call routine_done with that summary."
}
```

### `mode`: wake Barb, or start a new Barb

| `mode`  | In the app       | What a fire does                                                                                                                                                                                  |
| ------- | ---------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `wake`  | **wake**         | Types the task into Barb's **running** session when it is idle, so Barb keeps its context. Never starts a second Barb. If no Barb is running, starts one with the task as its first prompt. |
| `fresh` | **start a new**  | Starts a **new** Barb session every time, even if one is already running, with the task as its whole prompt. `overlap` decides what happens while the last run is still going.                |

Choose **wake** for an agent people keep open and talk to (a manager, a triage desk, a
long-lived builder). Choose **start a new** for independent jobs that want a clean slate
(a nightly report, a digest, a sweep), and for headless agents.

Pass `mode` explicitly. Left out, `routine_create` writes the agent's default: `wake` for a
visible routine on a saved agent that launches in the foreground, else `fresh`. The reply's
`effective_mode` says what a fire will do.

Wake has rules:

- It needs a **saved** agent. A built-in starter (`builtin/claude`, `builtin/codex`) is
  `fresh` only, so a tab someone opened by hand is never typed into.
- An agent that runs without permission checks (bypass or unattended) is woken only if its
  definition sets `allowWake: true`.
- A headless run is never woken. CodeSense can't tell when a Codex session is idle, so wakes
  into Codex sessions may come back `undelivered (unobservable)`.
- The wake text is the `task` with only `{{date}}` and `{{timestamp}}` filled in.
  `{{last_run_summary}}`, `{{last_run_at}}` and `{{trigger.*}}` fill in only for
  `fresh`; in a wake they stay literal, so don't rely on them there.

### `machine`: where Barb is looked for

`machine` is `local` (the default, this Mac), a machine id from `list_machines`, or `any`
connected machine. A wake on `any` goes into Barb's session wherever one runs, preferring an
idle one, and starts a new Barb on this Mac when none does. A remote wake is delivered by
the machine itself, so it lands even if the desktop drops while it waits. An `each_mac`
routine must use `machine: local` (or leave it out), except that a `fresh` one may use
`any` (each Mac then starts its own); a machine id is refused in either mode, since every
teammate's Mac would wake or start the same agent there.

A Barb on a machine that is offline still counts as running: the wake is `undelivered
(machine_offline)` and no second Barb starts while that machine stays offline.

### What a run says happened

While Barb is busy, a wake run is **queued** ("Waiting for Barb to be idle"). That is not
an end state: it waits up to the routine's max wait (`policy.max_wait`, 30 minutes by
default). A wake run ends as one of:

- **delivered**: typed into the session (the tab shows "Woken by ‹routine›" and a marker in
  the scrollback);
- **coalesced**: a fire that folded into one already queued;
- **undelivered (reason)**: nothing was typed, for example `busy_timeout`, `machine_offline`,
  `machine_unknown`, `session_ended`, `unobservable`, `needs_preparation`, `archived`,
  `limit_reached` (over the routine's `max_wakes_per_day`; it resumes on its own),
  `max_wakes` (the routine made its `max_wakes` and paused itself), `rate_limited` (the
  session's safety backstop; one inbox note per session per hour);
- **skipped (min_gap)**: inside the routine's `min_gap` with `overlap: skip`;
- **unknown**: it may have been delivered. CodeSense never re-sends an `unknown` delivery,
  and posts it once to the human inbox. Say "May have been delivered. Check the terminal
  before re-sending." Never re-send it yourself without looking.

A `fresh` run keeps its usual statuses (succeeded, failed, ended, timed out, needs you).

### The rest of `routine_create`

- `when`: a preset or a 5-field cron, in this Mac's zone unless `tz` (`Europe/London`):

  | The user says             | `when`                                   |
  | ------------------------- | ---------------------------------------- |
  | every 15 minutes          | `every 15m` (5m, 10m, 15m, 20m, 30m)     |
  | every 2 hours             | `every 2h` (1h, 2h, 3h, 4h, 6h, 8h, 12h) |
  | every hour                | `hourly`                                 |
  | every day at 9            | `daily 09:00`                            |
  | weekday mornings at 8:30  | `weekdays 08:30`                         |
  | Fridays at 5pm            | `weekly fri 17:00`                       |
  | the 1st of the month at 9 | `0 9 1 * *`                              |

  Nothing fires more often than every 5 minutes; for "every minute" use a timer. Omit `when`
  for a manual-only routine.
- `agent`: the agent's `id` in the routine's own space (`barb` is the team's agent for a
  team routine), or its full key from `agent_list`. Required unless you pass a `sessionId`
  launched as a saved agent, which then defaults to you. A team routine needs one of its
  own team's agents (or a starter, fresh only).
- `scope`: `team` (default, the active team) or `personal` (Only me, with `org`).
- `runsOn` (team only): `one_mac` (default; one shared job for the team) or `each_mac` (a
  recipe each teammate turns on for their own Mac with `routine_set_enabled`).
- `task` may use `{{date}}`, `{{timestamp}}`, `{{last_run_at}}`, `{{last_run_summary}}` and
  declared `variables` (`{"channel": {"type": "text", "default": "#web"}}` → `{{channel}}`),
  with the wake limit above.
- `dryRun: true` checks everything and writes nothing. Do it when unsure.

### Wake limits: you choose them for the work

Every limit is optional, set on the routine by whoever writes it (usually you). They count
wakes typed into a live session and are enforced by the terminal server that runs it, so
they hold on a connected machine with the desktop closed. What they do not cover:

- They apply to `mode: wake` only. A `fresh` routine starts a new agent each fire and makes
  no wakes; one with limits saves with a `wake_limits_ignored` warning (use `overlap`).
- A wake that finds no running agent and starts one (launch if absent) is not counted.
- Each Mac and machine keeps its own count: a `machine: any` routine has a budget per
  machine, and an `each_mac` recipe one per Mac.
- A machine whose terminal server is too old to enforce them is sent no limited wake: the
  run is `undelivered (unavailable)` with the reason as its detail, and the inbox is told
  once to update that terminal server. A machine-armed routine with limits is not armed
  there until it is (it fires nowhere meanwhile: the inbox says so once a day, and
  `routine_update` / `routine_arm_on` reply with a `wake_limits_unenforced` warning).

- `maxWakes`: wakes in all. Reached, the routine pauses itself and posts one inbox note;
  resuming it starts a new count.
- `maxWakesPerDay`: wakes in any rolling 24 hours. Fires over it end
  `undelivered (limit_reached)` and it resumes on its own.
- `minGap`: the least time between two wakes of this routine, into any session (`30m`, `2h`, `1d`, at
  most `7d`). A fire inside it is coalesced into the last one, or skipped with
  `overlap: skip`.

Light work needs none: a quick queue check can wake every 15 minutes for a week.

```json
{ "name": "Queue check", "agent": "barb", "mode": "wake", "when": "every 15m",
  "task": "Check the review queue. If it is empty, say so in one line and stop." }
```

Heavy work should not rewake or pile up:

```json
{ "name": "Regression sweep", "agent": "barb", "mode": "wake", "when": "hourly",
  "minGap": "4h", "maxWakesPerDay": 3, "overlap": "skip",
  "task": "Run the full regression suite and file what fails." }
```

`routine_update` takes the same three; `null` removes one. In the app they sit under
**Limits** in the routine's form, folded until opened. Separately, every session has a
fixed safety backstop (120 wakes an hour from all sources) that only catches loops.

Then tell the user what the reply says: `schedule_in_words`, the first of `next_fires`, the
`agent` and the `effective_mode`. Read `warnings`: the common one is a task starting with
`/name` the agent doesn't start with (fix with `agent_update`, adding the command or skill
to its `startup`).

### Event triggers

Set `events` in `routine_create` or `routine_update`, using the same event fields as
`routine.yml`, separate from `when`. Omitted or null events preserves; `[]` clears
inbox_idle, agent_done and role_pending; a nonempty list replaces those kinds only,
keeping schedules and metadata triggers.

```yaml
# config/agents/manager/routines/manager-wake/routine.yml
id: manager-wake
name: Wake the manager
owner: codesense
mode: wake
task: |
  You have unread mail. Call read_messages with your session id, then
  claim_role_messages for the manager role, and carry on with /manage-team.
where:
  kind: team_workspace
policy:
  max_runtime: 5m
triggers:
  - event:
      kind: inbox_idle   # one of the manager's sessions sits idle with unread mail
runs_on: each_mac
revision: 1
```

- `inbox_idle` fires when a session sits idle at its prompt with unread mail. With
  `mode: wake` only **the routine's own agent's** sessions fire it, and the one with the
  mail is woken; another agent's mail never wakes it. With `mode: fresh` any session the
  routine can reach (launched in its team) fires it, and `{{trigger.sessions}}` lists
  them. There is no middleman: do not write a routine whose agent calls `send_to_session`
  to wake another; give that agent its own wake routine. After 3 wakes that leave the
  same mail unread, the runner stops repeating that mail and records the reason in
  routine run history. Use `routine_runs` then `routine_run` to inspect it. Make it
  `runs_on: each_mac`: sessions are per Mac.
- `agent_done` (optionally `from_agent: reviewer`) fires when an agent finishes. A routine
  with it shows under the agent it runs, with an "after reviewer" note.
- In a `fresh` run, `{{trigger.sessions}}`, `{{trigger.count}}`, `{{trigger.session_id}}`,
  `{{trigger.status}}`, `{{trigger.summary}}` and `{{trigger.agent}}` say what fired it.

### Metadata triggers

Use `metadataTriggers` in `routine_create` or `routine_update`, not prose in `when`:

```json
{"id":"review-story","name":"Review changed stories","agent":"default","mode":"fresh","task":"Review the changed story and report the result.","maxRuntime":"5m","enabled":false,"dryRun":true,"metadataTriggers":[{"selection":{"where":{"kinds":["story"]}},"target":{"key":"status","op":"eq","value":"review"},"previous":{"key":"status","op":"eq","value":"in-progress"}}]}
```

Require `status: ok`, inspect `data.warnings`, and save by changing `dryRun` to false.
Omit `previous` for any entry into the target value. First discovery and restarts baseline
existing matches; they do not replay them. Metadata routines cannot use `each_mac`.
On update, omit `metadataTriggers` to preserve it; `[]` removes all metadata conditions.
The equivalent YAML is `triggers: [{event: {kind: metadata_change, metadata: {selection, target, previous}}}]`.
See the [complete cookbook YAML](../../../arc-g-routines/trigger-cookbook.html#metadata_change).

### Create and preview event triggers

Use `events: [{kind:"inbox_idle"}]` for unread mail at an idle prompt, or
`events: [{kind:"agent_done",from_agent:"reviewer"}]` for reviewer completion.
Only agent_done accepts `from_agent`; omit it for all agents in reach. The agent
reference needs valid syntax, not an installed agent.

Use `events: [{kind:"role_pending"}]` when a dispatcher needs every queue in reach.
Use `events: [{kind:"role_pending",role:"reviewer"}]` for reviewer mail only.
Only role_pending accepts `role`; it must be nonblank and needs no registry entry.
Preview creation with `dryRun:true`, inspect `data.triggers`, then save disabled
and read the definition with `routine_get` before enabling. Updates have no dry run.
Refusals identify `events[i].field` with a hint and save nothing. These three event
kinds support `each_mac`; metadata triggers still require `one_mac`.

The [cookbook](../../../arc-g-routines/trigger-cookbook.html#events) has equivalent
MCP and complete YAML examples. For a definition installed by hand, preserve placement,
open the app editor, make a harmless edit (such as the name), then choose **Save changes**
to validate it. Use `routine_arm_on {id, machine:"this_mac"}`
before enabling a `one_mac` routine. The schema browser's local shape check does not
establish event semantics. Role notification never claims mail: inspect `role_state`,
register and claim the queue, accept with `accept_role_message` before work, then
`ack_role_message` with the receipt after work. `send_role_message` sends role work;
`send_message` addresses a session or human.

### Command routines and chaining

For deterministic work use `action: command` and `command: [python3, scripts/check.py]`.
Each item is one argv element; no implicit shell, pipes, redirects or expansion. Commands
have no agent, task or mode, run on this Mac, and live under
`config/agents/_command/routines/<id>/routine.yml`. Program names use PATH. Keep scripts in the team content so teammates can run them;
program paths used as argv[0] must stay within that root. The working directory follows
`where.kind`: team content for `team_workspace`, or the managed clone for `repo:owner/repo`.
Set `maxRuntime` to bound execution.

Exit 0 succeeds; nonzero fails; cancelled and timed_out are separate outcomes. Read the
exit code and bounded stdout/stderr tails through `routine_runs` then `routine_run`.
The process gets `CODESENSE_ROUTINE_ID` and `CODESENSE_RUN_ID`; stdout becomes result_text.
A successor uses `after: {routine: check, on: succeeded}` in MCP or YAML. Create the
predecessor first, in the same space; cycles are refused. `on: finished` also continues
on unsuccessful terminal outcomes. The successor task or argv can use
`{{trigger.result_text}}`, `{{trigger.run_id}}`, `{{trigger.routine}}`, `{{trigger.phase}}`
and `{{trigger.detail}}`. `result_text` is what the agent produced; `detail` is CodeSense's
explanation of why the run ended (wake, machine and admission runs still use `result_text`).
See the [copyable metadata → command → agent chain](../../../arc-g-routines/command-routines.html#chain).
Choose an agent routine when the task needs judgment; use the
[agent design guide](../../../arc-e-agents/agent-design.html) for responsibilities.

## When a routine woke you, or started you

- **Woken** (`mode: wake`): the message starts with `[routine: <name> | run <id>]`. Do the
  task, then call `routine_done {sessionId, runId, outcome, summary}` to finish just that
  run. Don't call `signal_done` for it: that ends your whole session's task. If you call
  neither, the run is recorded `delivered`.
- **Started** (`mode: fresh`): the task is your whole prompt. Call `signal_done` with a
  `summary` when the routine wants a result (it becomes the next run's
  `{{last_run_summary}}`), or with status `needs-attention` and a question.
- Either way `routine_context {sessionId}` returns the routine, its pinned revision, the
  values your task was filled with and the last result.

The task is the whole contract: CodeSense adds nothing to it. Routines never deliver
results anywhere on their own: if the user wants a result posted, sent or written, the
task says so and names the tool.

## "What routines do I have", pause, change, run, delete

- `routine_list` (filter with `agent`) covers your private space and every synced team.
  Summarize each by name, agent, mode, `schedule_in_words`, enabled, `next_run_at` and
  how `last_run` went. `agent_get` lists one agent's routines. `routine_get` gives one in
  full with its last 5 runs; `routine_runs` has more history.
- Pause / resume: `routine_set_enabled`. It affects only this Mac's switch and is never a
  git change; a routine armed on another Mac is paused there.
- Change: `routine_update` with the `baseRevision` you last read and only the fields that
  change (`mode`, `machine`, `when`, `task`, …). `conflict` means re-read and reapply.
- Run once now: `routine_run_now`. Delete: `routine_delete` archives it; history stays.
  Archiving an agent archives its routines.
- Drafts: `routine_create` with `enabled: false`.

Anyone who can see a routine can change it. Edits are local edits to the context repo,
credited in its history; sharing them is a git push, which is yours to make when the user
wants it. Creating or changing a routine notifies no one.

People do all of this in the **Agents** tab: open an agent, and its **Routines** section
lists its routines as sentences ("Every weekday 9:00 · wake · Barb · on This Mac") with
**+ Add routine**. **Agents | Schedule** switches to a timeline of upcoming fires and recent
runs across agents, grouped by agent and machine. There is no separate Routines tab.

## Private dashboard results

For an agent-backed dashboard, `routine_create` accepts an inline JSON Schema in
`resultSchema` (`null` on update clears it). Bind the routine id to the page's
`routineResult`, `routineRefresh`, `routineStatus` and `routineCancel` (each takes `{key}`).
Cached reads never launch; make Refresh an explicit user action, and use
`onRoutineResult` to reread when a run finishes. The task must say: "Read `routine_context`
for the result schema, collect the data, publish `{sessionId, payload}` with
`routine_publish_result`, then call `signal_done` success." A candidate result is promoted
only on success; failure keeps the last good one. Never put credentials in a result.
Limits: schema 32 KiB, payload 1 MiB.

To fire while the desktop is closed, arm the routine on a machine with
`routine_arm_on { id, machine: <machineId> }`: schedule triggers only, `one_mac`, no `budget_usd`.

---
name: setup-machine
description: Get a remote machine ready for CodeSense over SSH — git, language runtimes, agent CLIs and a work folder — then test it from CodeSense. Use when the user says "set up my machine", "/setup-machine", "get this server ready for CodeSense" or "what's missing on <host>". Safe to rerun; it only installs what is missing.
---

# Set up a machine

You run on the user's Mac and set up a remote machine over SSH. You check first, install only
what's missing, and ask before anything that needs `sudo` or creates an account.

Rules:

- Every step is plain shell run as `ssh <host> '<command>'`. Check before you change:
  `command -v git` before installing git, `test -d ~/work` before `mkdir -p ~/work`. Running
  this skill twice must change nothing the second time.
- Ask before any command that uses `sudo`, and show the exact command first. If the user says
  no, print the command for them to run themselves and carry on.
- Never create, change or delete a Unix account here. That's the `add-machine-user` skill.
- Never ask for a password, token or key in chat, and never accept one. If `sudo` needs a
  password, ask the user to run that command in their own terminal.
- Keep it short: a line or two per step.

## 1. Connect

Ask which machine: the SSH host (an alias from `~/.ssh/config` or `user@host`) and the port
if it isn't 22. Check it answers:

```sh
ssh -o BatchMode=yes <host> 'uname -sm; . /etc/os-release 2>/dev/null; echo "$ID $VERSION_ID"'
```

If this fails, stop and help the user fix SSH first (their key, the host name, the port). Use
the OS and package manager you found (`apt-get`, `dnf`, `brew`) for every install below.

## 2. Check what's there

Run one check and show the user a short list of what's present and what's missing:

```sh
ssh <host> 'for c in git curl node npm python3 claude codex; do printf "%s: " "$c"; command -v "$c" || echo missing; done; test -d ~/work && echo "work: ~/work" || echo "work: missing"; printf "codex sandbox userns: "; cat /proc/sys/kernel/apparmor_restrict_unprivileged_userns 2>/dev/null || echo n/a'
```

Ask which runtimes their repos need (Node, Python, Go, Rust…) and which agent CLIs they use
(Claude Code, Codex, or both). Only install those.

## 3. Install what's missing

One item at a time, each only if its check said missing:

- **git and curl.** System packages, for example
  `sudo apt-get update && sudo apt-get install -y git curl`. Needs `sudo`: ask first.
- **Runtimes.** Prefer a per-user install that needs no `sudo` when the team uses one (a
  version manager such as `nvm`, `pyenv` or `rustup`). Otherwise the system package, after
  asking.
- **Agent CLIs.** Use each CLI's official install instructions. With Node present:
  `npm install -g @anthropic-ai/claude-code` and `npm install -g @openai/codex`. If a global
  npm install would need `sudo`, ask first or set a user prefix.
- **Codex's command sandbox (Linux, when Codex is used).** Codex runs each command in a
  sandbox built on user namespaces (bubblewrap). Ubuntu 23.10 and newer block those by
  default, and Codex then can't run any command ("Operation not permitted"). Check with
  `cat /proc/sys/kernel/apparmor_restrict_unprivileged_userns`. If it prints `1`, allow
  them, and keep it across reboots, with
  `echo 'kernel.apparmor_restrict_unprivileged_userns = 0' | sudo tee /etc/sysctl.d/60-codex-sandbox-userns.conf && sudo sysctl --system`.
  This needs `sudo`, so ask first. Then check with `cd /tmp && codex sandbox sh -c 'echo ok'`.
- **Work folder.** `mkdir -p ~/work`, or the folder the user names.

Each user signs in to their agent CLI themselves, on the machine. Never copy a login or an
API key onto it.

After each install, run its check again and report the version.

## 4. Test it from CodeSense

Call the `test_machine_connection` MCP tool with the machine:

```json
{
  "input": {
    "label": "<a short name>",
    "host": "<host or IP>",
    "port": 22,
    "username": "<user>",
    "signIn": { "method": "agent" }
  }
}
```

Pass `machineId` too when the machine is already in CodeSense (`list_machines` shows it).

The first test returns the machine's host key fingerprint. Show it to the user and ask them to
confirm it matches the machine. Only then call it again with that value as
`trustedHostKeyFp`. Report each step of the result in plain words, and the install plan if it
returns one.

If the machine isn't in CodeSense yet, tell the user to add it with **Machines → Add machine** in CodeSense, or
offer to save it with `save_machine` after they say yes.

## 5. Summary

List what was already there, what you installed, anything the user still has to run
themselves, and the test result.

Teams that already manage machines with Ansible can keep doing that. This skill is just the
plain-shell version of the same checks.
